news.title: Lawmakers confirm rule that benefitted Argentina was wrongly used at World Cup
news.lede: IFAB has admitted that VAR wrongly intervened on two instances of diving at the World Cup. One of them helped Argentina squeeze past Switzerland in the quarter-finals, setting up their win over England in the semis. Swiss forward Breel Embolo thought he had won a free-kick on the edge of the box following a tackle from Leandro Paredes. But the VAR recommended an on-field review on the basis of ‘mistaken identity’.

news.title: Were Argentina given preferential treatment at the 2026 World Cup? A explosive admission from the game’s law-makers
news.lede: The guardians of the international game have admitted that Argentina benefited from a contentious refereeing decision at the 2026 World Cup. At the centre of it all is the case of Breel Embolo. The former Bundesliga striker was sent off in the quarter-final of Switzerland's match against Argentina in the 72nd minute with the score at 1-1 after receiving a second yellow card. However, with the correct application of the rule adjustments introduced for the World Cup by the International Football Association Board (IFAB), that should never have happened.

news.title: NFL stadium used to host World Cup games completes major transformation back to football - 'welcome back'
news.lede: SOFI STADIUM has been given a makeover after hosting eight showdowns during the World Cup. The 70,240-capacity arena staged two USA clashes during the tournament, including the group-opening win over Paraguay. And Spain also featured at SoFi Stadium as they beat Belgium en route to being crowned World Cup champions. But the home of the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers is now back in NFL mode ahead of the new season.

news.title: The Real Reasons India Can't Reach the FIFA World Cup
news.lede: Despite its vast population, India's football World Cup dream remains a distant reality, plagued by deep-rooted systemic issues, a struggling national federation, and inadequate youth development, leaving fans to hope for a future turnaround. As the World Cup reached its final week, Gourav Roy, an Indian software engineer living in San Francisco, drove more than 6,000 miles across the United States to attend both semi-finals and the final. For Roy, it was the next best thing to what he had grown up dreaming of: seeing India play the World Cup. But the possibility of that dream coming true is looking ever more distant as deep-rooted systemic issues and the failure to implement reforms have left the country of 1.45 billion ranked a lowly 138th in the world, failing to even qualify for next year's Asian Cup.
